summary.title: bliki: Monolith First
summary.one_liner: Martin Fowler argues that new systems should usually start as a monolith and be split into microservices only once boundaries are clear and the need is proven.
takeaways: Successful microservice systems often began as a monolith that grew too big and was later split up; building greenfield microservices from scratch often caused trouble.
Microservices carry a 'microservice premium' (the cost of managing many services), which slows teams down, especially on simpler or unproven applications.
Hard-to-get-right service boundaries are easier to find in a monolith, since refactoring across services is much harder than within one codebase.
Monolith-first can be executed by building a modular monolith, peeling off services gradually, replacing the monolith entirely, or starting with a few coarse-grained services.
The counter-argument is that starting with microservices builds team habits and scaling structure, but Fowler advises against it without prior microservices experience on the team.
summary.summary: Fowler, writing in 2015, describes a pattern he hears from teams: successful microservice systems usually grew out of a monolith, while greenfield microservice builds often ran into trouble. He explains the reasons for a monolith-first strategy, including YAGNI, the microservice premium in speed, and the difficulty of getting service boundaries right early. He then lists several ways to execute the strategy and presents the opposing view that starting with microservices builds useful team habits. The piece is short, tentative in its conclusions, and cites anecdotes rather than hard data.
